report.summary: Detecting tests that rely solely on mocks involves three main techniques: mutation testing (e.g., deleting the implementation and checking if the test passes), coverage analysis (measuring how much of the module under test is actually executed), and assertion analysis (inspecting whether assertions only validate mock interactions). Mutation testing is the most reliable but computationally expensive, with tools like MutPy for Python. Coverage inspection is cheap and can be done per-commit using tools like coverage.py. Assertion analysis via static analysis is lightweight but may produce false p
risks: False positives: low coverage does not guarantee a test only tests mocks; it may test edge cases that happen to not cover lines.
Dynamic Python features and mocking frameworks (e.g., unittest.mock, pytest-mock) complicate static analysis of assertions.

Mutation testing may be too slow for per-commit feedback; on a moderate codebase, full mutation analysis can take minutes to hours, while targeted mutation (deletion of specific functions) may take seconds per test but requires careful selection.
Windows compatibility: some mutation testing tools (like mutmut) may have limited Windows support, requiring alternatives.
todos: Implement a per-commit pre-commit hook or CI step that uses coverage.py to check if a test module exercises the corresponding implementation module below a threshold (e.g., <X% line coverage) and flags it for manual review.
Integrate a heuristic that counts assertions on mock objects vs. real return values; if mock assertions dominate, raise a warning.
Set up a nightly mutation testing job (e.g., using mutmut or a custom script that replaces functions with mocks) to catch more subtle cases; store results for periodic audit.
For immediate triage, create a script that temporarily deletes the implementation module's body and re-runs tests to see if any still pass; this can be run manually on suspicious tests.

handoff.suggestion: Start with a coverage-based check: for each test file, require that the tested module's coverage is above a threshold (e.g., 5% statement coverage) or flag for review. This can be implemented via coverage.py with a simple configuration per commit. Combine with a mock-assertion ratio heuristic using AST analysis. Use mutation testing only as a periodic sanity check.

name: q21-tests-that-test-mocks
question: How do you mechanically detect a test that tests only its own mocks -- one that would pass with the implementation deleted? What tools or techniques exist (mutation testing, coverage of the module under test, assertion analysis), and what do they cost to run per commit?
